title: 200 core words
tomorrow: the Gita's first line has people 'wanting to fight.' which word?

segments.voice: Yesterday, 200 core words and maya: one school's appearance, another's wondrous power, in a single verse, each side heard at its best. Today, the plainest verbs of all: the body's.

Right now some sound is reaching your ears, something is under your hand, and your lungs are working without being asked. A busy body, quietly. Nobody narrates it; it just runs, all day, in the background. The Gita has a line that's nothing but that: a body's ordinary doings, one after another, like someone narrating a day. Seeing. Hearing. Touching. Smelling. Eating. Walking. Sleeping. Breathing.
screen: `A SOUND, A TOUCH, A BREATH.` → `A BODY, NARRATED.` → `SEEING. HEARING. BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, Gita 5.8: pashyan shrinvan sprishan jighrann ashnan gacchan svapan shvasan. Every word ends the same way, in -an, and that ending means while doing it. Pashyan, while seeing. Shrinvan, hearing. Sprishan, touching. Jighran, smelling, its n doubled before a vowel, one more join. Ashnan, eating. Gacchan, going. Svapan, sleeping. Shvasan, breathing. One is a relative of a word met before: gacchan grows from gam, to go, one of the roots from earlier. Now, what is the list doing? The first half of the verse says: naiva kinchit karomiti yukto manyeta tattvavit. The steady one, who knows the truth, thinks: I do nothing at all. Karomiti is karomi, I do, with iti, the closing quote mark. So the whole picture is a person seeing, hearing, eating, breathing, and still saying, inside, I'm not the doer here. The next verse gives the reason: the senses are moving among their objects. Some hear a teaching about not claiming every act as mine; some hear a picture of a calm person in the middle of ordinary life. Either way, for a reader of Sanskrit, the list itself is a gift: the body's core verbs, set out in a row, each one easy to spot by its ending. Learn the ending once, and a long string of verbs reads like a day: someone looking, listening, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing, all at once.
screen: `-AN: WHILE DOING IT.` · `PASHYAN, SHRINVAN, SHVASAN.` · `I DO NOTHING AT ALL.` · `THE SENSES MOVE AMONG THEIR OBJECTS.` · then, large: `THE BODY'S CORE VERBS.`

segments.voice: Go through the list with your own body, one per breath: look at one thing, pashyan; listen to one sound, shrinvan; touch what's under your hand, sprishan; smell the air, jighran. Then rest in the last word, shvasan, breathing, for the rest of the sit. Let the senses work; there's nothing to add.

Two hundred core words: today, the body's verbs, each ending in -an, while doing it: pashyan, seeing; shrinvan, hearing; sprishan, touching; shvasan, breathing. All of them done by a steady one who says, inside, I do nothing.
For the road: 200 core words, and the body says them all day long. Seeing, hearing, breathing, in Sanskrit.

notes: This stretch follows days 1463-1466 (to be; karma and phala; ca, eva, na, iti; roots kri, bhu, gam). Days 1467-1470 (roots; sukha and duhkha; datta; a review round) were read before the final pass; day 1471's hook answers 1470's tomorrow line (guessing a word from a known root).
Shape senses: the practice walks the listener through seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, breathing. Nani appears in the chat (the weekly elder).
Grammar: the -an forms are present participles (masc. nom. sg.); jighrann shows the doubled n before a vowel. Confirm.

Sanskrit is given in a simple romanization in the spoken text (no diacritics) so the voice can read it; the sources hold the same romanization. Confirm every word against a standard edition, and the verse numbers (editions differ by a verse around 1.27-1.28).
Grammar is described in plain words (endings, 'having done it', 'while doing it'); a Sanskritist should confirm each description.
